Gnat
năt
n. (the smallest unclean creature; half of Christ's proverb against the Pharisees)
From Old English gnaett. The Greek konops is the smallest of the unclean creatures, the camel the largest; the proverb depends on both being unclean by the law, so that the straining and the swallowing are the same kind of act at opposite scales.

Biblical Definition

Christ's charge against the scribes is not that they were too strict but that their strictness was selective: “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” (Matthew 23:24). The picture is of a man filtering his drink through a cloth to catch an insect too small to matter and then, in the same swallow, taking down the largest unclean animal in Palestine. The verse before gives the actual instance: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone” (Matthew 23:23). The last clause is the one most often dropped, and it settles the meaning. Christ does not tell them to stop tithing their herbs. He tells them they should have done the small thing and not left the great things undone. Precision is not the fault; the fault is a precision that never reaches judgment, mercy, and faith. Paul warns of a related failure in the assembly: “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears” (2 Timothy 4:3) — and James names what any such straining reliably yields: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (James 3:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the gnat as a small insect, or rather a genus of insects, the Culex — and notes the Scripture proverb of straining at a gnat.

expand to see more

GNAT, n. [Sax. gnaet.] A small insect, or rather a genus of insects, the Culex, with a proboscis armed with a sting.

GNAT, n. Any thing proverbially small; as, to strain at a gnat and swallow a camel.

STRAIN, v.t. To filter; to purify or separate from extraneous matter by filtration.

TITHE, n. [Sax. teotha, tenth.] The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock.

SCRUPULOUS, a. Nicely doubtful; hesitating to determine or to act, for fear of offending or doing wrong; cautious in decision.

Key Scripture

Matthew 23:24 — "Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel."

Matthew 23:23 — "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone."

2 Timothy 4:3 — "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;"

James 3:16 — "For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work."

Modern Corruption

The proverb is used to dismiss care about small obediences altogether, when Christ's own sentence commands the small thing and the great thing together.

expand to see more

Matthew 23:24 has become the standing proof-text for anyone who finds a scruple inconvenient. Somebody objects to a practice, and is told not to strain at gnats. Verse 23 makes that use impossible: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Christ affirms the herb tithe. What He condemns is a religion whose whole energy goes into the measurable small thing while judgment, mercy, and faith are left unattended. The proverb is not against precision; it is against a precision that has become a substitute.

The reason the figure works is that both creatures are unclean. The Pharisee straining his cup was obeying a real principle of the law and doing it carefully, and then swallowing a camel — the same uncleanness at maximum scale — without noticing. That is the permanent shape of the sin, and it is native to careful people. A church can conduct a two-year controversy over a matter of order while a member's family is destroyed by an unaddressed cruelty. Christ lists the three great matters by name so that no one has to guess which ones are the camels.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek konops (G2971), a gnat; kamelos (G2574), a camel; diulizo (G1368), to strain out; barus (G926), weighty.

expand to see more

Greek konops (G2971) — a gnat; only Matthew 23:24, the smallest unclean creature.

Greek kamelos (G2574) — a camel; unclean by Leviticus 11:4, and the largest beast at hand.

Greek diulizo (G1368) — to strain through; the filtering cloth over the cup.

Greek barutera tou nomou (G926) — the weightier matters of the law; judgment, mercy, faith.

Greek aphiemi (G863) — to leave, omit; what they did with the weightier matters.

Usage

"“Strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” — both unclean, at opposite scales."

"“These ought ye to have done” — the herb tithe is affirmed."

"“Judgment, mercy, and faith” — the camels, named so no one need guess."
